title: Kiowa County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Kiowa County wells have a 64-foot median depth. Review local yields, water levels, permit history and estimated finished-well costs of $8,200-$15,500.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Kiowa County
intro_html:
A well near Eads, Brandon or Sheridan Lake needs a parcel-level check, not just a county average. Kiowa County's recorded wells are generally shallow, but their permitted uses, producing formations and reported yields vary considerably.

Colorado DWR records contain 1,411 permitted wells in the county, with 731 recorded as constructed. Depth is reported for 819 wells, pump yield for 221 and static water level for 54. Those different sample sizes matter: the depth picture is much better documented than the water-level picture.

sections.heading: Most Kiowa County Wells Are Shallow, but the Parcel Sets the Depth
sections.html:
The median recorded depth is 64 feet, and the middle half runs from 46 to 92 feet. For an initial drilling budget, that puts the central range well below a deep-bedrock project. It does not promise that water will be available at that depth on your lot. Across the county, 77% of reported depths are under 100 feet, while the 90th percentile is 180 feet.

The cost model assumes alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. Permits name Ogallala for 99 wells and Dakota for 16; 1,216 sit in an unnamed/fractured-bedrock category. That broad label is not proof of fractured granite beneath a property. Ask the driller to compare nearby completion logs and identify the likely producing formation before setting a target depth.

sections.heading: Reported Yields Favor Useful Supply, Not a Guarantee at the Tap
sections.html:
Among the 221 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gpm, with a middle half of 10.0–50.0 gpm. Those figures suggest useful supply is common in the reporting sample, but the county combines household, stock and irrigation wells. A production figure from a different use or formation may be a poor comparison for a home site.

The reported share under 1 gpm is 0%, while 13% fall in the 1–5 gpm band. That lower band deserves careful attention to sustained output, household demand and storage. It does not establish an absence of weak wells or dry holes. Before buying, get a pumping test that documents drawdown and recovery rather than relying on the pump's rated capacity.

sections.heading: Kiowa County Water Levels Do Not Show a Countywide Decline
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to standing water before pumping, not the completed depth of the hole. Kiowa County's reported median is 46 feet below ground, and the middle half is 25–80 feet. A buyer should keep this separate from well depth when reviewing pump placement and available drawdown.

Decade medians move from 101 feet in the 1970s to 56 feet in the 2010s and 35 feet in the 2020s. These figures do not show progressively deeper standing water. They also do not prove the water table is rising: only 54 wells report static levels, and the measurements may represent different locations and formations. A trend at your property requires repeat measurements from comparable wells.

sections.heading: Permit Activity Reflects Kiowa County's Stock-Water Needs
sections.html:
Stock use appears on 52% of permits, compared with 26% for domestic/household use and 19% for irrigation. Treat those as recorded use categories, not mutually exclusive shares. For a buyer, the important point is that a nearby stock well is not automatically a model for a household permit or household demand.

Listed permit activity was highest in the 1990s, with 239 permits, versus 92 in the 2010s and 47 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025, so the latest decade is incomplete. The most active historical drillers are Hoffman (Hoffman, Earl), with 142 records; Kemp'S Well Service (Kemp, George), with 133; and Eastwood Drilling (Eastwood, Francis), with 95. These are historical counts, not confirmation of current availability.

sections.heading: Budget Beyond the Drilled Hole Near Eads or Sheridan Lake
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses $35–$55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 64-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,200–$3,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $8,200–$15,500. The hole alone is therefore not a useful total project budget.

Ask for a written scope covering casing, grout, development, pump equipment and the connection to the building. Confirm how the contractor handles extra footage, difficult ground and an unsuccessful hole. The 46–92-foot middle depth range helps frame an opening bid, but access, the actual formation and the distance to the house can change the finished price. These are modeled costs, not a parcel-specific quote.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality and Site Layout Before Committing
sections.html:
The environmental inventory lists 22 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund/cleanup site within about 10 miles. A mapped sampling location is not proof that a nearby domestic well is contaminated. Review the underlying site records and groundwater setting, then choose laboratory testing appropriate to the property. There are 0 mapped historic mine features, but that does not establish drinking-water safety.

Inspect the wellhead, casing and sanitary seal, and review available construction records. A yield report alone cannot establish potability or long-term reliability. For a new build, lay out the well, septic system, replacement septic area, driveway and house together. Keep required separations and drilling access workable before fixing the building location.

sections.heading: Buying a Kiowa County Lot: Verify the Well and the Permission
sections.html:
Start with the property's DWR permit and completion record, then compare neighboring wells around Eads, Brandon or Sheridan Lake. Match the formation, terrain and intended use as closely as possible. Cheyenne County and Prowers County offer broader regional context, but nearby records on the same groundwater setting are more useful than a distant county median.

A permit is not proof of a working well or permission for every use. Verify that the authorized uses cover the planned home, livestock or outdoor watering. Exempt household-use wells can carry restrictions, and some projects in over-appropriated basins may need augmentation. Make the purchase decision contingent on satisfactory records, water-quality testing, sustained-yield testing and a buildable well-and-septic layout.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Kiowa County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth is 64 feet, with the middle half between 46 and 92 feet. Of reported depths, 77% are under 100 feet, and the 90th percentile is 180 feet. Use those figures for preliminary budgeting, then compare nearby completion logs because the producing formation and depth can change across the county.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Kiowa County?
faq.a: The local model estimates drilling at $35–$55 per foot. At the 64-foot median depth, the hole is about $2,200–$3,500, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $8,200–$15,500. Get a written quote that specifies casing, grout, development, site access and what happens if more drilling is needed.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Kiowa County?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 15.0 gpm, and the middle half is 10.0–50.0 gpm. Only 221 wells report yield, and the sample includes different uses. Although the reported share under 1 gpm is 0%, 13% fall in the 1–5 gpm range. Test sustained output and recovery before relying on an existing well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Kiowa County?
faq.a: County permit records cannot establish whether a particular well is safe. The mapped inventory includes 22 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund/cleanup site within about 10 miles, but proximity alone does not prove contamination. Review relevant site records, inspect the well's sanitary condition and obtain laboratory testing suited to the property's potential exposures.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Kiowa County?
faq.a: The supplied decade medians do not show a dropping water table: reported static depths are 101 feet in the 1970s, 56 feet in the 2010s and 35 feet in the 2020s. However, only 54 wells report static levels, and these are not necessarily repeat measurements at the same wells. They cannot establish a countywide recovery either.
